<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<br class="ltx_break">through the Lens of Projection Geometry</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Compressing neural networks without retraining is vital for deployment at scale. We study calibration-free compression through the lens of projection geometry: structured pruning is an axis-aligned projection, whereas model folding performs a low-rank projection via weight clustering. We formalize both as orthogonal operators and show that, within a rank distance of one, folding provably yields smaller parameter reconstruction error, and under mild smoothness assumptions, smaller functional perturbations than pruning. At scale, we evaluate <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>1’000 checkpoints spanning ResNet18, PreActResNet18, ViT-B/32, and CLIP ViT-B/32 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, covering diverse training hyperparameters (optimizers, learning rates, augmentations, regularization, sharpness-aware training), as well as multiple LLaMA-family 60M and 130M parameter models trained on C4. We show that folding typically achieves higher post-compression accuracy, with the largest gains at moderate–high compression. The gap narrows and occasionally reverses at specific training setups. Our results position folding as a geometry-aware, calibration-free alternative to pruning that is often superior in practice and principled in theory.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Neural network compression is critical for deploying models in resource-constrained environments. Common approaches include quantization, which reduces the precision of weights and activations, and knowledge distillation, which transfers information from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. In this work, we focus on the class of calibration-free post-training structured compression methods that optimize the model architecture itself without access to training data. Among these, the most widely used is <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">magnitude-based pruning</em>, which prunes tensor elements according to their magnitudes, using them as a proxy for their contribution to model accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mishra et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bambhaniya et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. When combined with fine-tuning or a lightweight BatchNorm reset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saikumar and Varghese, 2025</a>)</cite>, this approach achieves significant compression rates with negligible accuracy loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kurtic et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanh et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
In contrast, the recently introduced <em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model folding</em> clusters similar weights and ties them together, providing an approximation of the original network <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Both pruning and folding reduce parameter count but differ fundamentally: pruning removes weights entirely, while folding preserves them in merged representations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we develop a unified theoretical and empirical framework to compare pruning and folding through the lens of <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">orthogonal projections</em> in parameter space. We show that both compression methods can be viewed as projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces, but with crucial differences in geometry: pruning corresponds to axis-aligned coordinate projections, while folding projects onto cluster-structured subspaces that retain directional information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">At a high level, both pruning and folding compress the weights of a model.
We show that for any pruned solution there exists a folded alternative that is <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">almost</em> as small—using one extra component in the compressed representation—yet is strictly closer to the original weights (smaller Frobenius norm), which in turn bounds the change in the network function.
Intuitively, folding merges weight vectors with similar directions rather than zeroing coordinates, so the compressed model stays closer in behavior to the initial network.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, we perform a comprehensive calibration-free study over <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>1’000 checkpoints spanning CNNs and ViTs on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, trained under diverse hyperparameter choices (optimizers, learning rates, augmentation, regularization, sharpness-aware training). We also train and process 18 LLaMA-family models with 60M and 130M parameters on C4, by varying learning rates, warmup lengths, and weight decay strength. After compression and also followed by lightweight and full fine-tuning, folding typically attains higher post-compression accuracy, with the largest gains at moderate to high compression. The margin narrows, and can occasionally reverse, at very low compression or under specific training setups, but the overall trend is consistent with our theoretical analysis. Our projection-based perspective opens new directions for designing compression methods that explicitly optimize for functional closeness. This paper makes the following contributions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a unified projection framework that casts pruning and folding as orthogonal projections onto, respectively, axis-aligned and cluster-structured subspaces. We prove that at a compression rank difference of one, folding achieves smaller parameter reconstruction error and tighter function-perturbation bounds under mild smoothness assumptions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A large-scale evaluation across <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>1’000 checkpoints and diverse hyperparameters, covering CNNs and ViTs on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, as well as LLaMA-60M and LLaMA-130M on C4. In addition, we use post-compression lightweight LayerNorm reset for ViTs, or full-fine-tuning to show that the strong performance of folding is preserved in these settings.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that folding is a geometry-aware alternative that is often superior in practice, with clearly identified regimes (<em id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, moderate–high compression) where its advantage is most pronounced, and corner cases where the gap narrows.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">We discuss related work in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Related Work ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>, however, the main text already positions pruning and folding within our projection framework and clarifies the novelty of our approach.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Preliminaries and Definitions</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a neural network with input <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. We assume ReLU activations and normalization layers (<em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, BatchNorm or LayerNorm) are present.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To develop the theoretical framework, we focus on compressing a single layer at a time. This layer has <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> inputs and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> outputs with its parameters collected in matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}</annotation></semantics></math>. A row <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(i)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(i)</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> is denoted as the <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>th parameter vector with individual weights <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(i,j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(i,j)</annotation></semantics></math>. Since all other network parameters are treated as fixed, the network function can be expressed as <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x;\bm{W})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑾</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x;\bm{W})</annotation></semantics></math>, which is trained to minimize a loss function <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L(\mathbf{W})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L(\mathbf{W})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We assume that the loss function <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is Lipschitz continuous, <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e.</em>, there exists a constant <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> such that</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|L(\mathbf{W}_{1})-L(\mathbf{W}_{2})|\leq\kappa\,\lVert\mathbf{W}_{1}-\mathbf{W}_{2}\rVert_{F}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|L(\mathbf{W}_{1})-L(\mathbf{W}_{2})|\leq\kappa\,\lVert\mathbf{W}_{1}-\mathbf{W}_{2}\rVert_{F}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">for all admissible parameter matrices <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. The Frobenius norm of a matrix is defined as <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert A\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert A\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>, that is, the square root of the sum of the squares of its entries, or equivalently, the <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-norm of the vectorized matrix.
This Lipschitz condition controls the change in loss with respect to parameter perturbations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Orthogonal Projection.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize structured pruning and model folding as orthogonal projections in parameter space. A matrix <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐂</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}</annotation></semantics></math> is an orthogonal projection if <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}^{\top}=\mathbf{C}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐂</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐂</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐂</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}^{\top}=\mathbf{C}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <em id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e.</em>, it is symmetric and idempotent. Such projections map any parameter vector to its closest point (in the Euclidean norm) within a lower-dimensional subspace.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">If the columns of <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}</annotation></semantics></math> form a basis of a <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspace, the corresponding orthogonal projection is</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{U}(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U})^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐂</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐔</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{U}(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U})^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Equivalently,</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}y=\underset{z\in\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{U})}{\arg\min}\;\lVert y-z\rVert_{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐂</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">z</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">∈</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">Range</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">𝐔</mi><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}y=\underset{z\in\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{U})}{\arg\min}\;\lVert y-z\rVert_{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">meaning <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐂</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}y</annotation></semantics></math> is the orthogonal projection of <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> onto the subspace spanned by <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐔</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Compression as Orthogonal Projection</h3>

<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Structured pruning.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Pruning can be viewed as a projection onto a coordinate-aligned subspace at the level of neurons, filters, or channels. Assume the layer outputs are ordered so that the last <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m-k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m-k</annotation></semantics></math> are pruned. The corresponding basis <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> spans the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspace, with projection matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and transformed weight matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I\\
0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf{C}_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I&amp;0\\
0&amp;0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mi>I</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mi>I</mi></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I\\
0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf{C}_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}I&amp;0\\
0&amp;0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Consequently, the last <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m-k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m-k</annotation></semantics></math> rows of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> are zero, and the corresponding neurons, filters, or channels can be simply removed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model folding.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Folding groups the parameters into <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> clusters and replaces each cluster with its mean. Depending on the choice of clusters, a different folding results. Folding can be represented as an orthogonal projection onto the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspace spanned by <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}_{f}\in\{0,1\}^{m\times k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}_{f}\in\{0,1\}^{m\times k}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each row contains exactly one nonzero entry indicating the cluster assignment. A cluster <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> comprises all indices of parameter vectors belonging to it; thus, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{f}(i,j)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{f}(i,j)=1</annotation></semantics></math> if and only if <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in S_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in S_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The projection <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> defined in Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Orthogonal Projection. ‣ 2.1 Preliminaries and Definitions ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> maps each cluster to its mean <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Specifically,</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{f}=\mathbf{C}_{f}\mathbf{W},\quad\forall i\in S_{j}:\;w_{f}(i)=\mu_{j},\quad\mu_{j}=\frac{1}{|S_{j}|}\sum_{i\in S_{j}}w(i)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.558em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{f}=\mathbf{C}_{f}\mathbf{W},\quad\forall i\in S_{j}:\;w_{f}(i)=\mu_{j},\quad\mu_{j}=\frac{1}{|S_{j}|}\sum_{i\in S_{j}}w(i),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean of cluster <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>. After projection, all parameter vectors within a cluster are replaced by their mean, making them identical. As a result, the corresponding layer outputs are also identical, leaving a total of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> distinct neurons, filters, or channels. Practically, the identical layer outputs can be joined while adapting the next layer appropriately, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Folding Dominates Pruning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To compare pruning and folding, we first show that for any choice of pruning, there exists a folding that yields a more accurate approximation of the parameter matrix <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Given any pruning with basis <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> of rank <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\leq k_{p}\leq m-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\leq k_{p}\leq m-1</annotation></semantics></math> (<em id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">i.e.</em>, at least one parameter vector is pruned), there exists a folding with basis <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> and rank <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}=k_{p}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}=k_{p}+1</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>
<table id="S2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> denoting the orthogonal projections defined in Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Orthogonal Projection. ‣ 2.1 Preliminaries and Definitions ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the above theorem, <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the constructive clustering obtained by merging all pruned rows into a single additional cluster. The proof is in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Proofs of Theoretical Claims ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. By the Lipschitz continuity of the loss function in Eq. <a href="#S2.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 2.1 Preliminaries and Definitions ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the superior approximation property of folding implies a tighter bound on the loss difference compared to pruning:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|L(\mathbf{W})-L(\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f})|\leq\kappa\,\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F},\quad|L(\mathbf{W})-L(\mathbf{W}_{p})|\leq\kappa\,\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|L(\mathbf{W})-L(\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f})|\leq\kappa\,\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F},\quad|L(\mathbf{W})-L(\mathbf{W}_{p})|\leq\kappa\,\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">with</p>
<table id="S2.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.1389em">≤</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, the rank difference <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}=k_{p}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}=k_{p}+1</annotation></semantics></math> between pruning and folding is practically negligible, since in typical scenarios many parameter vectors are pruned. For instance, under a uniform <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> per-layer retention, a ResNet-18 stage with 256 channels keeps <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}=128</annotation></semantics></math> (so folding uses <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}=129" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>129</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}=129</annotation></semantics></math>), and a ViT-B/32 block with width 768 keeps <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}=384" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>384</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}=384</annotation></semantics></math> (so <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}=385" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>385</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}=385</annotation></semantics></math>); the relative increase is just <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/k_{p}\approx 0.78\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>0.78</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/k_{p}\approx 0.78\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.26\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.26</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.26\%</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively—negligible in practice. Moreover, for all layers and architectures we observe that loss and accuracy vary smoothly as the rank increases from
<math id="S2.SS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}+1</annotation></semantics></math>, no jumps in loss or accuracy, and the error difference between ranks <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k+1</annotation></semantics></math> is typically much smaller than the difference between pruning and folding at the same rank (see Appendix <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Impact of one rank slack and singleton folding ‣ Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we show that folding using optimal <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means clustering never yields a less accurate approximation of the parameter matrix <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> than pruning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.2</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}^{\star}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}^{\star}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> be the basis obtained from an optimal <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means clustering with <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> clusters, <em id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">i.e.</em>, the folding clusters are determined by a <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means algorithm minimizing the accumulated within-cluster sum of squares. Then, for any pruning with basis <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> of rank <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}=k_{f}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}=k_{f}-1</annotation></semantics></math>, we have</span></p>
<table id="S2.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> denoting the orthogonal projections defined in Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Orthogonal Projection. ‣ 2.1 Preliminaries and Definitions ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The proof is given in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Proofs of Theoretical Claims ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. This result demonstrates that <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means folding is not merely a heuristic, but an optimal projection under clustering constraints. Note that the special folding <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> in Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 2.1. ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> is suboptimal, while Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2.2. ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> shows that <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> achieves the minimum possible reconstruction error over all clusterings, producing a strictly stronger improvement as <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0.1389em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Unlike pruning, which relies on parameter vector removal, folding generalizes the idea by enabling coordinated parameter merging. Thus, folding incurs less parameter distortion and provably smaller loss perturbation under a local parameter-Lipschitz assumption.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2.2. ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> has implications for a possible fine-tuning after compression. Matrix <math id="S2.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> contains the optimized weights and <math id="S2.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S2.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> contain the weights after pruning and folding the optimized network. As a result of Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2.2. ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, the quadratic distance between the optimized weights and the compressed optimized weights is smaller for folding in comparison to pruning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our theoretical results employ a one–rank slack comparing pruning at rank <math id="S2.SS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> to folding at <math id="S2.SS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}=k_{p}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}=k_{p}+1</annotation></semantics></math>, as a proof device to obtain a clean monotonicity guarantee on projection error. This slack does <em id="S2.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> reflect our evaluation protocol. In all experiments we enforce matched sparsity budgets and compare methods at the <em id="S2.SS3.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">same</em> retained size (parameters and FLOPs). Hence, empirical accuracy gaps cannot be attributed to extra capacity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S2.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Folding outperforms magnitude pruning across diverse training regimes.</span>
<span id="S2.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top row:</span> ResNet18 and PreActResNet18 on CIFAR-10. ResNet18 checkpoints were trained from scratch with Adam using different hyperparameter configurations. PreActResNet18 checkpoints are from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andriushchenko et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
<span id="S2.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom row:</span> ViT-B/32 on CIFAR-10 from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andriushchenko et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and CLIP ViT-B/32 on ImageNet-1K from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>. See Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Training Details ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for details. In these plots, we use checkpoints that were trained without L1 regularization. Scatter plots show post-compression accuracy for magnitude pruning (L1 criterion) versus folding at uniform per-layer compression ratios (color-coded by layer-wise compression ratio). Bar plots depict the accuracy gain by folding, computed as <math id="S2.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{FOLD} })}-\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{MAG1} })}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Acc</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">FOLD</mtext><mtext> </mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>Acc</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">MAG1</mtext><mtext> </mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{FOLD} })}-\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{MAG1} })}</annotation></semantics></math>, as a function of layer-wise compression ratio. Folding yields the largest improvements at moderate to high compression, confirming its robustness across architectures and datasets. Fig. <a href="#A4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ D.1 ResNet18 on CIFAR-10 Training Setup with Adam and SGD ‣ Appendix D Training Details ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows the results for magnitude pruning with L2 criterion.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Most pruning studies vary only seeds by training several checkpoints under a single hyperparameter recipe, leaving the role of upstream training underexplored. We instead benchmark <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>’000 checkpoints spanning diverse hyperparameters (optimizers, learning rates, augmentation, regularization, SAM) to quantify how training choices interact with folding and pruning. Concretely, we train 216 ResNet18 (Adam) and 576 ResNet18 (SGD) models on CIFAR-10, include 50 PreActResNet18 and 200 ViT-B/32 checkpoints from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andriushchenko et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and add 72 CLIP ViT-B/32 models fine-tuned on ImageNet-1K from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>. The two ViT families differ markedly in scale (<math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>19M vs. <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>151M parameters). We also train 36 LLaMA-family 60M and 130M parameter models on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Raffel et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Training details are in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Training Details ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>. The results for LLaMa-130M are in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S3.F3.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Folded models retain their accuracy advantage after fine-tuning.</span> Results for ResNet18 trained by Adam on CIFAR-10 (<span id="S3.F3.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">top row</span>) and CLIP-ViT-B/32 trained on ImageNet-1K (<span id="S3.F3.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bottom row</span>): <span id="S3.F3.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a,d)</span> compares post-compression accuracy of magnitude pruning (<span id="S3.F3.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span>) versus folding (<span id="S3.F3.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span>) after 1 and 5 epochs of fine-tuning. <span id="S3.F3.18" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b,e)</span> show the accuracy gap between folding and pruning as a function of fine-tuning epochs, demonstrating that folding maintains a consistent lead, <em id="S3.F3.19" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e.</em>, the <span id="S3.F3.20" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> accuracy delta is positive. <span id="S3.F3.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c,f)</span> illustrate accuracy trajectories before and after 5 epochs of fine-tuning for both methods, highlighting that folded models recover accuracy faster. Further results in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Extended Empirical Comparison of Folding and Pruning ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We empirically compare model folding and structured pruning across CNNs, ViTs and LLaMA-60M models under matched training setups. Unless stated otherwise, we do not apply gradient-based fine-tuning: for CNNs we only re-estimate batch-normalization statistics via a single forward pass using <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">REPAIR</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jordan et al., 2023</a>)</cite> to isolate structural effects, and ViTs / LLaMA-60M models are left uncalibrated. Note that <span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">REPAIR</span> was recently shown to substantially improve post-compression performance for pruned models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saikumar and Varghese, 2025</a>)</cite>, and has also been applied on top of folding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We report results (i) immediately after compression (CNNs after <span id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">REPAIR</span>, ViTs with no further step), (ii) for ViTs additionally after a LayerNorm reset, and (iii) for both families after 1–5 epochs of full fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Folding vs. Structured Pruning on CNNs and ViTs.</span>
We compare model folding (<span id="S3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span>) with structured magnitude pruning (<span id="S3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG</span>) under L1 and L2 criteria (<span id="S3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span>, <span id="S3.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG2</span>) across representative CNN and ViT architectures. Fig. <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes results: scatter plots show accuracy of <span id="S3.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> vs. <span id="S3.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> for each trained model, with compression ratio indicated by color. Results for <span id="S3.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG2</span> are in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Extended Empirical Comparison of Folding and Pruning ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>. Box plots depict the distribution of accuracy differences between <span id="S3.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> and <span id="S3.p3.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span>. Positive differences indicate folding outperforms pruning, with the gap widening at higher sparsity. This trend holds across ResNet18, PreActResNet18, ViT-B/32, and CLIP ViT-B/32 on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, demonstrating robustness to architecture and dataset scale. These results support our theoretical claim (Sec. <a href="#S2" title="2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>): folding projects onto cluster-structured subspaces, preserving parameter alignment and reducing functional distortion, yielding consistent accuracy gains over magnitude pruning.</p>
