<td id="S3.T1.2.1.19.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.19.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">29.57</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.19.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.19.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">54.43</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.19.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.19.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">47.77</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.19.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.19.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">351.11</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.19.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.19.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">209.06</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S3.T1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation of <span id="S3.T1.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> and <span id="S3.T1.12.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG2</span> on LLaMA-60M.</span> We train and evaluate 18 LLaMA-family models with 60M parameters on C4 by varying max_lr, warmup steps and weight decay. Columns 4–8 show perplexity of the trained model before compression and after pruning / folding using layer-wise pruning ratio of <math id="S3.T1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math>. We prune only FFN blocks. Except for low learning rates with long warmup schedules, <span id="S3.T1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> outperforms <span id="S3.T1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG2</span> (highlighted in bold).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance Comparison after Lightweight and Full Fine-Tuning.</span>
The previous results isolate structural effects by evaluating models without further optimization. We now test whether folding’s advantage persists after fine-tuning.
Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> compares <span id="S3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> and <span id="S3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> on ViTs under lightweight LayerNorm-only adaptation: across ViT-B/32 (CIFAR-10) and CLIP ViT-B/32 (ImageNet-1K), folding consistently reaches higher post-compression accuracy, with the gap <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}(\texttt{FOLD})-\mathrm{Acc}(\texttt{MAG1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Acc</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">FOLD</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>Acc</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">MAG1</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}(\texttt{FOLD})-\mathrm{Acc}(\texttt{MAG1})</annotation></semantics></math> remaining positive and typically growing with compression.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we allow brief fine-tuning (1–5 epochs).
Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that folded models (a,d) start from higher accuracy and retain their lead, (b,e) maintain a positive relative gap, and (c,f) recover faster with fewer plateaus.
Thus, folding provides a better initialization and requires fewer updates to regain performance, making it advantageous in settings with limited fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance Comparison on LLaMA-60M.</span>
Tab. <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Experimental Results ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> evaluates <span id="S3.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> and <span id="S3.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG2</span> on LLaMA-60M trained on C4 under 18 hyperparameter settings (varying learning rate, warmup, and weight decay). We prune or fold only the FFN blocks and report perplexity at baseline and at 20% and 50% layer-wise sparsity. Except for models trained with very low learning rates and long warmup, <span id="S3.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> consistently outperforms <span id="S3.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG2</span>. Similar finding have been obtained for LLaMA-130M models in Tab. <a href="#A6.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Model Compression Ablation Studies</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The previous sections demonstrated that folding often outperforms structured pruning across architectures and compression ratios. On ResNets and ViTs, we probe which training factors impact this advantage. Specifically, we analyze sensitivity to learning rate, the use of sharpness-aware training (SAM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foret et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, regularization and data augmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Prabhu et al., 2019</a>)</cite>—the hyperparameters known to influence loss landscape geometry and generalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fort and Jastrzebski, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Neyshabur et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>)</cite> in non-trivial ways <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andriushchenko et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. To validate these curvature-related hypotheses, Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> includes a sharpness analysis. Our measurements quantify how hyperparameters shift the local geometry of the loss landscape and help explain when <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> ’s advantage widens or narrows.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/resnet/sgd__compression_ratio_scatter__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/resnet/sgd__compression_ratio_hist__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimizer effect</span> evaluated on ResNet18 checkpoints trained on CIFAR-10 with SGD (no L1 regularization). The figure complements Fig. <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Role of Optimizer.</span>
We repeat the ResNet18 analysis under Adam and SGD to gauge optimizer sensitivity. Compared to the Adam-trained sweep in Fig. <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a), the complementary SGD sweep in Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4 Model Compression Ablation Studies ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the same qualitative ordering—<span id="S4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> exceeds <span id="S4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> across compression levels—but with different baselines and dispersion: SGD checkpoints form a tighter cloud and exhibit a smaller median gap, whereas Adam yields larger variance and at times a more pronounced <span id="S4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> advantage, especially at higher compression.
The <span id="S4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span>–<span id="S4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> difference remains positive under both optimizers in most cases, but its magnitude is optimizer-dependent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effect of Learning Rate.</span>
Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4 Model Compression Ablation Studies ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> reports post-compression accuracy for <span id="S4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> versus <span id="S4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> across learning rates on ResNet18 (Adam, SGD), PreActResNet18, and ViT-B/32. With Adam, <span id="S4.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> ’s edge is largest at moderate–low rates, narrows and can reverse at very high rates, and vanishes again at extremely small rates (both methods degrade). For SGD, the dependence is weaker and can be inverted (<em id="S4.p3.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, ViT-B/32).
The effect of learning rate is expressed through sharpness (see Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>): when training places the model in regions where folding produces a smaller sharpness increase than pruning, folding wins. When folding produces a larger sharpness increase (most visible at high learning rates under Adam), pruning can outperform.
Adaptive methods like Adam are associated with sharper minima and distinct generalization behavior compared to SGD, amplifying this sensitivity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wilson et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jastrzębski et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S4.F5.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning rate modulates folding’s edge.</span> Post-compression accuracy of <span id="S4.F5.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> and <span id="S4.F5.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> across learning rates: ResNet18 with Adam <span id="S4.F5.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> and SGD <span id="S4.F5.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span>, PreActResNet18 <span id="S4.F5.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span>, and ViT-B/32 <span id="S4.F5.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d)</span>. <span id="S4.F5.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> leads at moderate–low rates. With Adam, the gap shrinks or reverses at very high rates, and closes again at extremely small rates. SGD shows weaker or opposite dependence.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effect of SAM.</span>
Fig. <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4 Model Compression Ablation Studies ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> evaluates training with and without SAM and measures post-compression accuracy. Across models, SAM lifts both methods.
With light L1 regularization (<math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>) during training shown in (b), pruning narrows the gap at <em id="S4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">low</em> compression (where induced sparsity aligns with L1), yet <span id="S4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> regains and extends its lead as compression increases. These trends are consistent with the view that SAM steers training to flatter solutions, reducing curvature sensitivity.
Within this flatter neighborhood both pruning and folding projections operate inside the same robustness ball, so their geometric differences matter less and the gap narrows—an effect stronger for ViT-B/32, where high <math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> homogenizes head / channel saliencies and reduces the relative advantage of clustering.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S4.F6.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/preactresnet/preact_resnet__sam_scatter__MAG1_vs_FOLD_l1_0.0.png" id="S4.F6.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/preactresnet/preact_resnet__sam_hist__MAG1_vs_FOLD_l1_0.0.png" id="S4.F6.sf3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(c) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S4.F6.sf4" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/vit/vit__sam_scatter__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F6.sf4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/vit/vit__sam_hist__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F6.sf4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(d) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="S4.F6.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SAM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foret et al., 2021</a>)</cite> can boost model compression.</span> Post-compression accuracy under training with / without SAM. <span id="S4.F6.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> ResNet18 (Adam), no L1. <span id="S4.F6.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> ResNet18 (Adam), L1<math id="S4.F6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="S4.F6.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span> PreActResNet18 (SGD), no L1. <span id="S4.F6.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d)</span> ViT<span id="S4.F6.18" class="ltx_text">-</span>B/32, no L1. SAM improves both <span id="S4.F6.19" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> and <span id="S4.F6.20" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span>, but the uplift is consistently larger for <span id="S4.F6.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span>, especially with Adam. Light L1 regularization helps <span id="S4.F6.22" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> at low compression, yet <span id="S4.F6.23" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> retains a clear advantage at moderate–high compression.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effect of Data Augmentation.</span>
Fig. <a href="#footnote2" title="Footnote 2 ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 4 Model Compression Ablation Studies ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> plots the distribution of <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>Accuracy <math id="S4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\texttt{FOLD}-\texttt{MAG1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">FOLD</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">MAG1</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\texttt{FOLD}-\texttt{MAG1})</annotation></semantics></math> across checkpoints versus the layer-wise compression ratio, contrasting runs without (gray) and with RandAugment (green). For ResNet18 (Adam and SGD) and PreActResNet18, RAUG reduces or shifts <span id="S4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> ’s relative benefit. In contrast, for ViT-B/32 RAUG increases <span id="S4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> ’s advantage: the median <math id="S4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> rises with compression, suggesting that augmented ViT representations are especially amenable to projection-based removal. A plausible mechanism is that augmentation biases training toward flatter, more invariant solutions. This is supported by our sharpness analysis in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> and consistent with recent theory linking augmentation-induced input perturbations to equivalent parameter-space perturbations and showing that augmentations bias training toward flatter minima <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoo and Yoon, 2025</a>)</cite>.
Standard augmentation (<span id="S4.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">augm=True</span>) shows a similar trend and is omitted for brevity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="S4.F7.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/resnet/adam__raug_hist__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F7.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="S4.F7.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/resnet/sgd__raug_hist__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F7.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="S4.F7.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/preactresnet/preact_resnet__raug_hist__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F7.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(c) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="S4.F7.sf4" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18116v1/fig/vit/vit__raug_hist__MAG1_vs_FOLD.png" id="S4.F7.sf4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:115/115;" width="115" height="115" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(d) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span><span id="S4.F7.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Augmentations have a generally positive effect on the post-compression accuracy.</span>
Post-compression accuracy without / with random augmentations for <span id="S4.F7.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> ResNet18 (Adam), <span id="S4.F7.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> ResNet18 (SGD), <span id="S4.F7.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span> PreActResNet18, and <span id="S4.F7.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d)</span> ViT-B/32.
Augmentations boost both <span id="S4.F7.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> and <span id="S4.F7.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span>. On ResNet18 they also narrow <span id="S4.F7.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> ’s advantage—most noticeably at moderate compression—consistent with added invariances making axis-aligned removals less damaging.
In ViT-B/32, augmentations are essential for folding<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Note that the base accuracy of ViT-B/32 checkpoints trained without RAUG is lower than with RAUG.</span></span></span>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">These ablations reveal a consistent pattern: conditions that encourage flatter and structured solutions—moderately low learning rates and SAM with a small–moderate radius—magnify <span id="S4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> ’s advantage, whereas extremes reduce it: very high or very low learning rates, stronger augmentations, or large SAM radii narrow the gap; SGD generally dampens all effects relative to Adam. This aligns with our projection view (Sec. <a href="#S2" title="2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>): when weights are well aligned, clustering reduces projection error more than coordinate removal and thus perturbs the function less, while weaker alignment or broad robustness neighborhoods make the two projections behave more similarly.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion, Limitations, and Outlook</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We framed structured pruning and model folding as projection-based compression and showed that folding achieves smaller parameter deviation with a one-rank slack, implying tighter functional preservation under mild smoothness. A calibration-free evaluation over <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>1’000 checkpoints (ResNet18, PreActResNet18, ViT-B/32, CLIP ViT-B/32; CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K; and LLaMA-60M and LLaMA-130M on C4) found that <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FOLD</span> typically surpasses <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MAG1</span> in post-compression accuracy, with the clearest gains at moderate–high compression and under training conditions that induce flatter, more structured solutions (<em id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, moderate learning rates, SAM). The gap narrows at very low compression and can shrink under strong data augmentation or large SAM radii, but the overall trend is robust across optimizers and hyperparameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations.</span>
Our theoretical guarantee allows a one-component increase in compressed rank but does not establish universal dominance at exactly matched sizes. Empirically, we focus on standard CNN and ViT families on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, as well as small LLaMA models on C4. For ViTs and LLaMA, pruning and folding are applied only to the FFN blocks. Extensions to attention layers is left for future work. We evaluate in strictly calibration-free settings, with optional BatchNorm/LayerNorm resets and short fine-tuning budgets, and compare primarily against magnitude-based structured pruning. Interactions with quantization, distillation, and unstructured sparsity are not considered. Larger LLMs are beyond the scope of this study due to the computational cost of training across diverse hyperparameter settings. We note that most SoTA pruning methods for LLMs rely on calibration data (<em id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, activation-aware/second-order) and are exclusively pruning-based.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Outlook.</span>
We plan to extend folding to pruning / folding attention blocks, calibration-based settings and evaluate on larger LLMs / VLMs. We also plan to study interactions with quantization and adaptation methods. More broadly, our projection-based view positions folding as a geometry-aware primitive for compression: a foundation on which novel calibration-based compression methods, hybrid pipelines with quantization and distillation can be built, and a step toward principled model compression framework. In this sense, folding is not only a practical tool but a building block for the next generation of compression methods tailored to foundation models and deployment at scale.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reproducibility Statement.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our compression operators and evaluation protocol are described in Sec. <a href="#S2" title="2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>-Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Experimental Results ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, with ablation studies in Sec. <a href="#S4" title="4 Model Compression Ablation Studies ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. A repository with configs and scripts to regenerate all figures/tables is linked in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Code, Data, and Resources ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. Complete proofs are in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Proofs of Theoretical Claims ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. Related literature is summarized in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Related Work ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. Training setups, datasets, links to the used checkpoints, and hyperparameter grids in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Training Details ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>, and extended results in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Extended Empirical Comparison of Folding and Pruning ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>. Our limited LLM usage statement is in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Use of Large Language Models ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>. Together, these materials enable re-running the full pipeline and regenerating the results.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Appendix</h2>

<div id="Ax1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Ax1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The following sections provide supplementary information and complement the main paper:</p>
<ul id="Ax1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="Ax1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Ax1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Code, Data, and Resources</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Code and logs.</span>
A repository with all source code, experiment configs, and figure-generation scripts (including the exact logs used to render every plot/table) are released at <a href="https://github.com/osaukh/folding_as_projection" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/osaukh/folding_as_projection</a>. The repo contains: implementations of folding and pruning operators, training/evaluation pipelines, scripts to plot ablations, and notebooks to reproduce figures directly from logs. We log all training metrics and hyperparameters with Weights &amp; Biases<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Weights &amp; Biases: <a href="https://wandb.ai" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://wandb.ai</a></span></span></span> and export logs alongside the code for reproduction. Additionally, we provide another repository for reproducing results of compressing LLaMA-60M and LLaMA-130M with folding and magnitude structured pruning at <a href="https://github.com/nanguoyu/simple_model_folding_public" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/nanguoyu/simple_model_folding_public</a>. Our folding implementation is based on the code by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite><span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          Model folding universal: <a href="https://github.com/nanguoyu/model-folding-universal" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/nanguoyu/model-folding-universal</a> and model folding for CNNs: <a href="https://github.com/marza96/ModelFolding/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/marza96/ModelFolding/</a></span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets.</span>
We use CIFAR-10<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          CIFAR-10: <a href="https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar.html</a></span></span></span> and ImageNet-1K<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          ImageNet-1K: <a href="https://image-net.org/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://image-net.org/</a></span></span></span>. CIFAR-10 is downloaded automatically via <span id="A1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torchvision</span>. ImageNet-1K requires the official credentials and follows its license. Pretrained/fine-tuned checkpoints referenced in the paper are either trained by us (configs in the repo) or obtained from the cited works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andriushchenko et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>. The download links are also provided in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Training Details ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compute resources.</span>
Experiments were run on a cluster featuring 8<math id="A1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> NVIDIA A100 (80 GB RAM) GPUs. All random seeds are fixed in the configs and scripts.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Computational complexity and memory cost.</span>
At inference and matched retained sizes, folding and structured pruning yield the same compute and memory. The difference lies in the compression step: magnitude pruning is a one-pass scoring and selection procedure (<math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(pm)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(pm)</annotation></semantics></math> to score <math id="A1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> filters of dimension <math id="A1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, plus <math id="A1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(p\log p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(p\log p)</annotation></semantics></math> selection), whereas folding runs <math id="A1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means on layer weights with <math id="A1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> sweeps. Using Hartigan’s algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hartigan and Wong, 1979</a>)</cite>, one sweep costs <math id="A1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(pkm)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(pkm)</annotation></semantics></math>, with max <math id="A1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=10</annotation></semantics></math> sweeps the total is <math id="A1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(pkmT)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(pkmT)</annotation></semantics></math> (effectively linear in <math id="A1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">pm</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="A1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is small). This cost is paid once per layer and is small compared to training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Runtime overview.</span>
The most expensive step in our study is fine-tuning of CLIP VIT-B/32 on ImageNet-1K (1–5 epochs), which dominates wall-clock time (order of hours per run). In contrast, compression is lightweight. We detail measured runtime overhead of compression in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Additional Analyses: Sharpness, Runtime, and LLMs ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Proofs of Theoretical Claims</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Below we prove that for any choice of pruning, there exists a folding that yields a more accurate approximation of the parameter matrix <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.1</span></span><span id="A2.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Given any pruning with basis <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> of rank <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\leq k_{p}\leq m-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\leq k_{p}\leq m-1</annotation></semantics></math> (<em id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">i.e.</em>, at least one parameter vector is pruned), there exists a folding with basis <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> and rank <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}=k_{p}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}=k_{p}+1</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>
<table id="A2.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> denoting the orthogonal projections defined in Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Orthogonal Projection. ‣ 2.1 Preliminaries and Definitions ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A2.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">The rows of <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> can be ordered such that the pruned parameter vectors are first: <math id="A2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(1),...,w(m-k_{p})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(1),...,w(m-k_{p})</annotation></semantics></math>. Then we find that</span></p>
<table id="A2.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

0\end{pmatrix}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">using Eq. <a href="#S2.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ Structured pruning. ‣ 2.2 Compression as Orthogonal Projection ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. For the existence proof, we choose a folding that clusters all parameter vectors <math id="A2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(1),...,w(m-k_{p})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(1),...,w(m-k_{p})</annotation></semantics></math> into a single cluster, all other parameter vectors have individual clusters, <em id="A2.p2.2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e.</em>,</span></p>

</div>
<div id="A2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The following theorem shows that folding using optimal <math id="A2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means clustering never yields a less accurate approximation of the parameter matrix <math id="A2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> than pruning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.2</span></span><span id="A2.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}^{\star}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}^{\star}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> be the basis obtained from an optimal <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means clustering with <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> clusters, <em id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">i.e.</em>, the folding clusters are determined by a <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means algorithm minimizing the accumulated within-cluster sum of squares. Then, for any pruning with basis <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> of rank <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}=k_{f}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}=k_{f}-1</annotation></semantics></math>, we have</span></p>
<table id="A2.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}=\mathbf{C}_{p}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}=\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{\star}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> denoting the orthogonal projections defined in Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Orthogonal Projection. ‣ 2.1 Preliminaries and Definitions ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A2.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text">According to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bauckhage (2015)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, the problem of <math id="A2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means clustering can be formulated as the following constrained matrix factorization problem:</span></p>
<table id="A2.Ex13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{\mathbf{U}}\;\left\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{U}(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U})^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\quad\text{subject to}\quad u(i,j)\in\{0,1\},\;\sum_{j}u(i,j)=1\;\forall i." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>𝐔</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.280em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐔</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.280em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.447em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\mathbf{U}}\;\left\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{U}(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U})^{-1}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\quad\text{subject to}\quad u(i,j)\in\{0,1\},\;\sum_{j}u(i,j)=1\;\forall i.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text">This formulation coincides with the orthogonal projection of model folding, see Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Orthogonal Projection. ‣ 2.1 Preliminaries and Definitions ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and Eq. <a href="#S2.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ Model folding. ‣ 2.2 Compression as Orthogonal Projection ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Theorem <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 2.1. ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> guarantees the existence of a folding basis <math id="A2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> and the corresponding projection <math id="A2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}^{\prime}_{f}</annotation></semantics></math> for any pruning <math id="A2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="A2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that</span></p>
<table id="A2.Ex14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\;\;\geq\;\;\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.838em" rspace="0.560em">≥</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{p}\rVert_{F}^{2}\;\;\geq\;\;\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p6.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text">Since optimal <math id="A2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-means clustering achieves the minimal possible error <math id="A2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}\;\;\leq\;\;\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.838em" rspace="0.560em">≤</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\star}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}\;\;\leq\;\;\lVert\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{f}\rVert_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, the theorem follows.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model compression encompasses a wide range of approaches designed to reduce inference cost while preserving model utility. We focus on <em id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">post-training, calibration-free structured compression</em>, where the model architecture is modified without access to data or gradients. In this setting, the dominant baselines are structured pruning and, more recently, model folding. Below we discuss these families of methods and clarify how our projection-theoretic view relates to and extends prior work.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Post-training compression.</span>
Quantization reduces arithmetic precision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Darvish Rouhani et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, but typically requires calibration to maintain activation ranges. Knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hinton et al., 2015</a>)</cite> produces reduced students trained to imitate teacher logits. Even data-free variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Micaelli and Storkey, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Haroush et al., 2020</a>)</cite> require full training dynamics and do not yield structural compression. Low-rank factorization via matrix or tensor decompositions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren and Zhu, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horvath et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lebedev et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2016</a>)</cite> approximates pretrained weights by continuous subspaces but generally requires fine-tuning for restoration. These approaches differ fundamentally from our objective: they modify numerical precision or parameterization, not the discrete structure of the model.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structured pruning.</span>
Structured pruning removes neurons, channels, filters, or blocks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al., 2016</a>)</cite>. Magnitude-based criteria <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Entezari and Saukh, 2020</a>)</cite> dominate due to simplicity and hardware alignment. However, structured pruning typically requires fine-tuning or recalibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kurtic et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanh et al., 2020</a>)</cite> to mitigate accuracy degradation, and even calibration-based methods such as SparseGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frantar and Alistarh, 2023</a>)</cite> or Wanda <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite> operate through axis-aligned removal of coordinates. One-shot improvements using N:M sparsity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang, 2020</a>)</cite> or OT-based structural alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Theus et al., 2024</a>)</cite> still operate within the same paradigm: pruning corresponds to enforcing that the retained parameter vectors lie in a fixed coordinate-aligned subspace.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our work shows that such axis-aligned projections are geometrically restrictive. We formalize pruning as an orthogonal projection onto a coordinate subspace and demonstrate that, at matched ranks up to one slack, pruning is provably dominated by projections onto cluster-structured subspaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weight clustering and model folding.</span>
Model folding, recently introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, ties groups of similar channels by replacing them with their mean, yielding dense low-rank layers that preserve structural couplings. Folding implicitly performs a <em id="A3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cluster-structured projection</em> determined by discrete assignments, and practical implementations rely on k-means clustering. This operator class is strictly richer than axis-aligned pruning: folding enables coordinated merging rather than coordinate removal, while remaining compatible with dense inference. IFM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is related in that it also merges channels via grouping, but its variance-collapse correction is ineffective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, leading to substantially weaker performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our work strengthens this line along two axes. First, we provide a unified <em id="A3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">projection-geometric framework</em> showing that both pruning and folding are orthogonal projections, but onto fundamentally different subspaces: coordinate-aligned versus cluster-structured. Second, we prove that for any pruned solution of rank <math id="A3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a folded solution of rank <math id="A3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\!+\!1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.052em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\!+\!1</annotation></semantics></math> with strictly smaller parameter reconstruction error, and that optimal k-means folding minimizes this projection error among all cluster-structured projections. This establishes a strict theoretical separation between pruning and folding and explains the empirical superiority of folding in calibration-free settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model merging and alignment.</span>
Model merging combines independently trained models via parameter averaging or permutation alignment. Model soups <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2022a</a>)</cite> exploit shared initialization. Permutation matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Entezari et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ainsworth et al., 2023</a>)</cite> constructs neuron correspondences. REPAIR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jordan et al., 2023</a>)</cite> stabilizes fused models by re-normalizing preactivations. Intra-model merging approaches such as ZipIt! <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stoica et al., 2024</a>)</cite> combine computational units but do not target compression under fixed architectural constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">These works differ from ours in both objective and mechanism. Merging seeks functional fusion across networks, whereas folding compresses a <em id="A3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">single</em> network by exploiting intra-layer redundancy. Our projection-theoretic formulation shows that folding operates as a structured projection with explicit geometric optimality guarantees—properties not shared by merging methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Positioning of this work.</span>
Across pruning, folding, and merging, prior efforts lack a unifying mathematical framework that characterizes the geometry of post-training structural compression. Our contribution is to introduce such a framework: we cast pruning and folding as orthogonal projections and show that cluster-structured projections admit strictly smaller distortion than coordinate projections under practically negligible rank slack. This perspective yields nontrivial theoretical guarantees and aligns closely with the empirical phenomena observed across CNNs, ViTs, and LLaMA models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Training Details</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The following subsections detail the hyperparameters used to train our checkpoints. For checkpoints taken from the literature, we summarize the available training details.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>ResNet18 on CIFAR-10 Training Setup with Adam and SGD</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We trained a total of 792 ResNet18 models on CIFAR-10 by varying hyperparameter configurations. We used two optimizers: Adam and SGD. Tab. <a href="#A4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ D.1 ResNet18 on CIFAR-10 Training Setup with Adam and SGD ‣ Appendix D Training Details ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes the parameter combinations explored for each optimizer. For Adam, we used 3 learning rates and 1 momentum value. For SGD, we used 3 learning rates and 2 momentum values. The remaining parameters were shared across both optimizers: weight decay (3 values), L1 regularization (2 values), RandAugment (2 values), Sharpness-Aware Minimization (3 values), and learning rate scheduling (2 values). This resulted in 216 models trained with Adam and 576 models trained with SGD. In the ablation studies, we filter checkpoints (as specified in the figure captions) to highlight the observed effects.</p>
</div>

</tbody>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span><span id="A4.F8.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Folding outperforms magnitude pruning across diverse training regimes.</span> The same setup as in Fig. <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.3 Folding Dominates Pruning ‣ 2 Unified Framework for Pruning and Folding ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, but compared to the L2 magnitude pruning criterion.
<span id="A4.F8.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top row:</span> ResNet18 and PreActResNet18 on CIFAR-10. ResNet18 checkpoints were trained from scratch with Adam using different hyperparameter configurations.
<span id="A4.F8.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom row:</span> ViT-B/32 on CIFAR-10 and CLIP ViT-B/32 on ImageNet-1K. Scatter plots show post-compression accuracy for folding versus magnitude pruning (L2 criterion) at uniform per-layer compression ratios. Bar plots depict the accuracy gain by folding, computed as <math id="A4.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{FOLD} })}-\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{MAG2} })}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Acc</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">FOLD</mtext><mtext> </mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>Acc</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">MAG2</mtext><mtext> </mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{FOLD} })}-\mathrm{Acc}{(\text{{MAG2} })}</annotation></semantics></math>, as a function of layer-wise compression ratio. Folding yields the largest improvements at moderate to high compression, confirming its robustness across architectures and datasets.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>PreActResNet18 on CIFAR-10</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use 50 trained PreActResNet18 models on CIFAR-10 from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andriushchenko et al., 2023</a>)</cite><span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Download link: <a href="https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1LmthJCb3RXBFWjeTOC4UOOl7Ppgg2h7n" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1LmthJCb3RXBFWjeTOC4UOOl7Ppgg2h7n</a></span></span></span>. The models are trained using a fixed set of training parameters and a sweep over a few key hyperparameters. Tab. <a href="#A4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ D.2 PreActResNet18 on CIFAR-10 ‣ Appendix D Training Details ‣ Cut Less, Fold More: Model Compressionthrough the Lens of Projection Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> summarizes varied parameters used in this experiment. All checkpoints used the same training protocol: 200 epochs, batch size 128, and no label noise. The model width was fixed at 64 and the learning rate schedule followed a cyclic pattern. Only the maximum learning rate (<span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lr_max</span>), SAM strength (<span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">sam_rho</span>), and augmentation settings were varied. For the learning rate ablation studies, we adopt the reported maximum learning rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F9" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
